title: The other half of the plan
intro: Decumulation, the look-once-a-year discipline, and the rupee question nobody spends an evening on.

steps.title: The accumulation obsession
steps.body:
Indian personal finance has one great obsession: **accumulation**. The SIP is 'almost a civic virtue'; the journey from monthly savings to corpus is celebrated 'with near-religious enthusiasm.'

The gap: **very little attention to what happens after the corpus is built** — investors are taught to accumulate, not to live off it with confidence.

steps.title: The Desi Retirement Plan
steps.body:
Kaeley's corrective, distilled:

- The central question: **'Will your money outlive you, or will you outlive your money?'**
- Retirement is **a life stage, not a numerical milestone**.
- Money must be split **by job** — different pools for different tasks; one pool can't do every job at once.
- **Healthcare gets special attention** — in India, medical costs are the retirement wildcard.

steps.title: Look once a year — field-tested
steps.body: Last month's column ('a fund portfolio, once assembled with care, is best left largely unwatched') drew a reader's proof: the argument travels beyond funds. The discipline is the same one the [fund side](#/pack/finance-mfi-2026-09/concept/portfolio-checkups) formalized as the yearly four checks — attention is a cost, not a virtue.

steps.title: The rupee's working lifetime
steps.body:
Early 1980s: **₹9 per dollar**. Today: **~₹96**. Over one working lifetime the rupee lost **more than 90%** of its dollar value — 'yet most Indian investors have never spent a single evening asking why.'

> [!tip] The portfolio consequence: long-term rupee goals silently carry this leak. Some hard-currency-linked earning power — exporters, global funds — is the hedge hiding in plain sight.

recap:
**Accumulation is half a plan.**

- Decumulation: money split by job; healthcare is the wildcard; life stage, not milestone.
- Look once a year — the discipline transfers from funds to everything.
- ₹9 → ₹96: a ~5.5%/yr leak most portfolios never price.
- The question that organizes it all: will the money outlive you?
